text: 7. 15. Your toast pops up.
You've already picked the jam, already planned your day. Twice.
Your little sister bursts in.
Max, where's my left shoe? You don't even look up. Under the couch. Behind the blue bag. She checks.
It's there. She stares at you. That's creepy.
Maybe, but you're only... thinking.
At school, your teacher writes a problem on the board.
12 numbers, four steps.
She turns to ask the class. You're already done. You raise your hand. 418. Silence.
Your best friend Leo leans over.
Mate, did you even look at it? You did. For about one second.
Which, for you, felt like 10.
At lunch, a boy drops his tray. Everyone gasps.
You see the fork, the cup, the soup, the exact spot where it will land. You step aside. Easy.
The soup misses your shoes by one centimeter. Leo claps slowly. Show off.
Back home, your sister wants tea. You pour the water. You plan her birthday. You rewrite your essay.
You solve a crossword in your head.
You even name your future dog.
And your tea is still brewing. Here's the thing.
A normal brain is busy, but it isn't fast.
A nerve signal travels at up to about 120 meters per second.
Your eyes jump about three times a second.
A person talks at roughly 150 words a minute.
And a normal human needs about a quarter of a second just to react to a flash of light.
That's the speed of the world.
Slow, patient, comfortable. Now look at yours.
One morning, nobody knows why, your brain wakes up running 10 times faster.
Same skull, same you, 10 times the speed.
A normal person gets one thought. You get 10.
A normal second becomes 10 seconds of thinking.
A normal minute becomes 10 minutes. But there's a rule.
Your brain got 10 times faster. Your body did not. Your legs did not. Your eyes did not.
Your stomach definitely did not.
And the world certainly did not.
You can't move faster.
You can only decide earlier.
So what if you could think 10 times faster? Let's start small.
A pencil rolls off a desk.
A normal hand starts moving after the pencil has fallen 30 centimeters.
Yours starts after three.
You catch it before it's really falling. Leo stares.
Okay, that's not fair.
Plus, you never drop anything again. Next, exams. One hour on the clock.
You read every question in minutes.
You know every answer.
But your pen still writes at normal speed.
So you finish early and your brain just sits there waiting for your hand.
The teacher frowns.
Max, why are you staring at the ceiling? Because I'm done. Twice. Then chess club. Blitz.
Three minutes each.
For you, that's 30.
You see five moves ahead. Then eight.
The school champion shakes your hand. His fingers tremble. How did you do that? You shrug.
I just had more time. Plus. But here's the minus.
People talk slowly. Painfully slowly.
Leo sounds like a record on the wrong speed.
So you finish his sentences. Wrong half the time.
Max, let me finish! Minus. You're getting annoying.
Reading is the same trap.
Your brain understands a page in a blink.
But your eyes still jump only three times a second. Always.
A novel still takes hours.
Your brain reads a page, then waits.
Like a sports car in traffic. Basketball next.
Coach fires a ball at your face.
A normal player sees it, decides, and moves in about a quarter of a second.
You, two and a half hundredths. You catch it one -handed. Coach blows the whistle. You knew where it was going.
Physics. Don't be smart.
But you still can't run faster than the others. You just start earlier. Then the track meet. The gun fires. You're gone.
Beep! False start! Here's the rule.
React faster than a tenth of a second, and officials decide you must have guessed. You didn't guess.
You just heard it ten times faster. Nobody believes that. Plus. You're quick. Minus. You're disqualified. Dr.
Lee, your old physics teacher, now works at the City University.
He gives you a problem his team couldn't solve in a year. You finish it over lunch. Between sandwiches. He drops his coffee.
You catch it. Of course you do.
You fix the school bus timetable on a napkin.
Eleven minutes saved on every route.
The principal nearly cries. Sports day. Dodgeball.
Twelve balls fly at once. You see every arc.
You know where each one lands.
You take one step, and every ball misses you.
The class goes quiet. Your gym teacher whistles. Max! You're cheating! I'm just early. Plus. You win.
Minus.
Nobody picks you for their team anymore. Quiz night.
Leo's team gets the capital of Australia. You know in a flash. Canberra. Not Sydney.
A normal team argues for a minute.
You wait ten minutes for them to agree on the wrong answer. Then arguments.
Your brain finds the perfect reply in a blink. And the next. And the next.
You win every single one. Plus. You're always right. Minus. You're losing friends. Music is next.
You try the guitar. You read the song once.
Your brain knows every note. Every chord. Every finger. Your fingers? Not a chance.
Muscles learn at muscle speed. They need weeks.
Your brain is a genius in a very slow body. The catch?
You can't skip the practice.
Languages are the same story.
You understand Spanish grammar in an afternoon.
But new words don't stick faster.
Your brain files memories while you sleep.
And sleep still takes eight hours. Even for you. Online games next.
You plan 20 moves in a blink.
But your hand clicks at hand speed.
The top player still beats you.
His fingers have 10 ,000 hours.
Yours have 10 minutes. Then cooking.
You plan every step.
The pasta still takes 10 minutes.
Water still boils at 100 degrees.
It takes as long as it takes.
You stare at the pot like it owes you money. Now the road. A car runs a red light.
A typical driver needs about one and a half seconds to see, decide, and break. You decide in a flash.
But the car still needs distance to stop.
Physics doesn't care how smart you are.
And waiting is torture.
An elevator ride of 20 seconds feels like more than three minutes.
A red light of one minute feels like 10.
At the dentist, a 10 -minute wait feels like 100.
The world plays like a movie in slow motion. And you can't skip ahead.
Then comes the big idea.
You sit in the library and think.
In one afternoon, you plan a bridge, a cure, a better battery, a week of thinking in a single day. Dr.
Lee reads your notes.
Max, this is brilliant!
But a lab test still takes weeks.
Bacteria grow at bacteria speed.
Concrete still needs about 28 days to cure.
Your mind can race ahead of the world.
It just can't drag the world with it.
The world has its own clock, and you don't own it. Then the headaches begin.
Three days at full speed.
You squint at every light. Your temples throb. Dr. Lee checks your pulse. 80 beats a minute. Normal.
But your brain is a marathon runner stuck in a sprint. Sleep, he says. Max, sleep!
Then there's the cost. Hunger.
Your brain is about 2 % of your body weight.
It burns about 20 % of your energy.
That's around 20 watts.
10 times faster means around 200.
A whole resting body runs on about 100. So you eat. Breakfast. Second breakfast. Third.
Leo counts. That's your fifth sandwich.
It's my brain's fifth sandwich.
And still, you're hungry.
At night, your stomach growls so loud your sister bangs on the wall. Quiet! Some of us are sleeping! You are not.
Your brain is replaying Tuesday.
For the ninth time. Then the clip.
Leo films you catching three pens at once. Posted as a joke.
By morning, 40 ,000 views.
By lunch, 200 ,000.
Comments say, fake. Edited. Maybe real.
And one comment, from an account with no photo, says, Very impressive, Max. We'd love to meet you. Wait.
They know your name.
Here's the part nobody warns you about. Boredom. Not the sleepy kind.
The loud kind.
Deep in your brain, a small group of cells release dopamine.
They fire hardest, not when something is good, but when it's better than expected.
A reward you predicted barely makes them whisper. Now think about your brain. You predict everything. The punchline.
The plot twist. The cake in the box.
What your mom will say before she opens her mouth.
So the spark never lights. Not once. A birthday party.
You knew about it three days ago. A movie.
You know the ending in 10 minutes. A song.
You hear the next note before it plays.
Your favorite song feels like a calendar. Even jokes. Leo starts one. You already know the end.
You smile anyway. Politely.
It's the smile you've practiced. Then come the nights.
Your thoughts don't turn off. They replay your day. Again. And again.
10 times before midnight. Your head pounds.
Your hands shake when you skip a meal. And you hide it all.
You count to two before you answer. You pause on purpose.
You fake a frown when someone asks something simple.
Being normal is hard work.
It's like walking in slow motion through a crowd that thinks you're just walking.
And somewhere out there, someone is watching your clip again. Slowly. Frame by frame. Taking notes.
Then there's Mia. Your sister. 11 years old.
Dinner is her favorite time. She tells you about her day. Slowly. Every detail.
The substitute teacher. A shoe that squeaked.
You've guessed the ending by her second sentence. But you listen anyway.
Her voice is the only sound that feels like real time.
And she is the only person in the world you can't predict.
One night, she announces she wants a hamster. You guessed pizza. Wrong.
She says the hamster should be named Doctor.
You never saw that coming. Not even a little.
And for one heartbeat, something flickers. A tiny spark. Then it's gone.
When she was five, thunder terrified her. So you invented a game.
If you ever yell pancake, she drops flat on the floor and rolls toward your voice. Fast. Safe. Straight to you.
Silly but sweet. She's 11 now. She still does it. After rolling her eyes.
Her school talent show is on Friday.
In the Old City Theater.
She has four minutes of the worst jokes in town.
Every evening, she practices in the kitchen.
Every evening, you listen.
And every evening, you know what's coming. Tonight, she finishes. Ta -da! You clap.
She looks at you. You didn't laugh. You used to laugh.
Now you just… wait. Her voice is small. Come Friday, okay? Sit in the back. Don't leave.
You promise.
Above your desk hangs her drawing.
A boy with a giant head and tiny legs.
Under it, my brother, the brain.
The legs, she says, are the funny part.
Later, you lie awake. You count her jokes. 41. You know everyone.
You'd give a lot to be surprised by just one. Dr.
Lee gives you three rules. Eat. Sleep.
And if anyone offers you a fortune, record every word.
On Wednesday, a gray car stops at your gate.
A tall man in a gray coat steps out. Mr. Black. Holden Institute. We saw your clip.
His smile is perfect. Too perfect. Two million. A private lab. A team.
All the food you can eat. You'd live on sight. What about my sister? She can visit. Weekends. Maybe.
He slides a contract across the table. Sign by Friday. Read it fast. We know you can. He laughs at his own joke.
You press record on your phone. Quietly. Dr. Lee would be proud.
Friday, 7 p .m. The Old City Theater. Gold curtains. Dusty velvet.
You sit in the very last row, 30 meters from the stage, because you promised.
You skip dinner to finish Mia's costume. Your stomach growls.
Leo sits beside you.
And in the third row, a gray coat. Mr. Black. Waiting. Mia walks on stage. Center.
Spotlight. She tells her first joke. The crowd laughs. You don't. You're scanning. You always are.
20 meters above her hangs the lighting rig. A steel frame. 12 heavy lights. Then you hear it. Tink.
A tiny sound.
A normal ear hears nothing.
You hear arithmetic. A cable strand. Snapping. Tink. Two. Tink. Three.
Your blood goes cold.
16 strands hold that rig. Five are gone. Now six. Seven.
The rest will give way in about one second. One second. For you, 10. Your thoughts sprint.
Your body stays in the chair.
A rig falling 20 meters takes two seconds.
It hits at nearly 70 kilometers per hour.
Mia is right beneath it. Smiling.
You are 30 meters away.
A fit teenager sprints about eight meters per second. 30 meters? Nearly four seconds.
Stairs, seats, legs. Not enough. Not even close.
Ten times the thinking gives you a hundred plans.
Not one of them has legs.
Every plan ends the same way. Too late. Your brain got faster. Your legs didn't.
You scan the room like a map. Row 12. Row 11.
A man with a giant popcorn tub.
A child on the aisle.
40 steps to the stage.
Each one a chance to trip. A hundred plans.
A hundred ways to be late. Your chest tightens.
Your thoughts have never felt so slow. Think!
Your vision goes gray at the edges. Your hands shake.
Your brain is starving.
200 watts and no dinner. Think!
Sound travels about 340 meters per second.
30 meters takes nine hundredths of a second.
Your legs are too slow. Your voice isn't. But what do you shout? Look out!
Panic makes people freeze.
She would need a quarter of a second just to hear it.
Then more time to understand it. Too slow.
You need a word that needs no thinking.
A word she's heard a hundred times.
A word that sends her toward you. And then you see the price.
If you shout now, everyone will turn.
Everyone will wonder how you knew. Mr. Black will know. The cameras will know.
Your normal life will be over.
Stay quiet and your secret stays safe.
Shout and she stays alive.
The secret or the sister? There's no third option. You stand on your chair. Anyone can be fast.
There's only one Mia. Pancake! The theater turns. Mia freezes. One tenth.
Two tenths.
Then she drops. Flat. She rolls. Toward your voice. Toward the edge. Over it.
Into the empty front row.
The rig hits the stage where she stood. Steel. Glass. Dust. Silence. Then screaming.
Your knees fold. The room goes dark. Leo catches you.
You wake up on the carpet with a sandwich in your hand. Leo shoved it there. Mia is alive. A scraped elbow.
A torn costume. That's it.
She crashes into you so hard you almost fall again.
How, how did you know? She whispers. You say nothing. You look around. Phones are up. Dozens.
All recording.
And a gray coat is already walking down the aisle. Mr. Black. Smiling. That was extraordinary.
Come with us.
We'll make sure nobody bothers you.
Your family will be taken care of. Two million. Sign tonight. You could do something else. You could outthink him.
Outsmart every lawyer in his building. Ruin him in a day.
But then you'd be just like him.
Instead you do the simplest thing. You tell the truth. Dr. Lee pushes through the crowd.
Out of breath holding the contract. He's read it twice. Clause 9.
Subject remains on site. Indefinitely. Clause 14. Phase 3. Acceleration.
They don't want to study him. Dr. Lee tells the room. They want to push him.
His brain already burns about 200 watts.
Push it harder and it overheats. And starves. Silence. You hold up your phone. You press play.
Black's voice fills the theater. She can visit. Weekends. Maybe. A mother gasps.
A reporter lifts her notebook.
The manager crosses his arms. Mr.
Black's perfect smile cracks. He steps back. Then back again. Then he leaves.
Nobody chases him. Nobody needs to.
The truth is heavy enough.
Real offers never rush you.
And real contracts never hide the exit. Read twice. Always. Leo pats your shoulder.
Mate.
You just beat the smartest man in the room.
By not being clever at all. You nod.
For once you don't plan your answer.
You just feel it.
The manager apologizes to Mia. To the crowd. To you.
Then Mia asks to finish her act. Right there. On a broken stage.
The crowd sits back down.
She tells her last joke. Everyone laughs. Even Leo. Even Dr. Lee.
Later you and Mia sit on the edge of the ruined stage. Her feet swing.
By morning your clip has two million views.
But nobody is talking about the cable.
They're talking about one word. Pancake.
Mia hands you another sandwich. Eat. You obey. She grins. Hey Max. Want to hear a joke? Sure.
You'll know it. You always do.
What did the pancake say to the ceiling? You open your mouth. Nothing. No idea.
For the first time in months. No idea. Nothing. She says. It fell flat.
One second. Two. Then something warm. Something bright.
The spark finally lit up. You laugh. Loud. Messy. Ugly. Right on time.
And Mia laughs even harder.
Because she hasn't heard that sound in a year. Anyone can be fast.
There's only one Mia. Now what's real?
Let's separate fact from fiction. Fact.
Your brain weighs about one and a half kilograms.
It holds roughly 86 billion neurons.
It burns about 20 watts. Fiction.
No human has ever thought 10 times faster. Fact.
Nerve signals top out near 120 meters per second.
That's a speed limit built into the wiring. Fact.
Most people react in about a quarter of a second.
Athletes shave a little off.
Nobody gets near two and a half hundredths. Fact.
In 2007, David Eagleman's team dropped volunteers from a tall tower into a net.
Everyone said time slowed down.
But when tested, they couldn't read any faster.
Fear didn't speed up the brain.
It made the memory heavier. Fact.
In the 1990s, Wolfram Schultz and colleagues found that dopamine cells respond most to surprise.
Real science, real boredom. Fiction. The pancake trick.
Please don't test it on your sister.
So could a brain really keep getting faster? Forever?
That night, your laptop turns on by itself. A message appears. Good evening, Max. Not Halden.
Someone better. Quick question.
Have you ever wondered if you're the fastest?
Before you can answer, a photo loads. A girl your age.
Sitting in a glass room. Eyes closed. Wires on her temples. Underneath. Her name is Nova.
She thinks a hundred times faster than you. And she's asking for you.
You look at the clock on the wall. It ticks.
Slower than it did this morning. Much slower. You blink.
And somewhere inside your head.
Something just sped up. What do you think? Tell us in the comments.
And tell us which superpower we should do next.
Hit like and subscribe for part two.
